answer: The demographic transition theory explains how the population of a region changes over time as it moves from a rural, agrarian and illiterate society to an urban, industrial and literate one. It describes this change in three main stages.

answer.text: In the first stage, both the birth rate and the death rate are high, and they roughly balance each other. As a result the population remains low and stable. This is typical of a poor, agrarian society with little medical care.

In the second stage, better food, sanitation and medicine cause the death rate to fall sharply, while the birth rate remains high. This creates a rapid rise in population, often called the population explosion.
In the third stage, as society becomes urban and educated, the birth rate also falls to match the low death rate, and population growth slows down and becomes stable again.

answer: Thus the theory links population growth to the stage of a society's economic development.

questions.q: What factors affect the distribution and density of population across the world?

answer.text: is very unevenly distributed, and several factors decide where people live thickly or sparsely.

list: Geographical factors: fertile plains, moderate climate, fresh water and mineral wealth attract people; deserts, dense forests and high mountains repel them
Economic factors: industrial areas, mines and cities with jobs draw dense populations
Places with good housing, education and health attract settlers
Stable, peaceful regions hold more people than those torn by conflict, so river valleys and industrial regions are the most densely peopled

questions.q: What are the causes and consequences of rapid population growth in the world?

answer.text: has grown very fast in recent times, driven mainly by a fall in death rates while birth rates stayed high.

list: Better medicine, food and sanitation cut death rates sharply
In many developing countries birth rates remained high, so numbers rose rapidly
It puts pressure on land, water, food, jobs and services, and can worsen poverty and environmental damage
But a young, growing population can also be an asset if it is educated, healthy and employed
